title: The Lord with a towel
sum: The second half of John's Gospel opens. The public signs are over; from here to the cross Jesus speaks only to his own. At supper, the night before Passover, he gets up, strips to a towel and washes his disciples' feet, the job of a slave. Peter refuses, then wants a full bath. Jesus explains: unless he washes them, they have no share with him; and as their Lord and Teacher has served them, they owe the same service to one another.

The mood darkens. Jesus is shaken and announces that one of them will hand him over. At Peter's prompting the disciple Jesus loved, who appears here for the first time, asks who it is. Jesus gives Judas a dipped piece of bread; Satan enters Judas, and he goes out into the night. Then Jesus begins his farewell: now the Son of Man is glorified. He gives a new command, to love one another as he has loved them, and warns Peter that before the rooster crows he will deny him three times.
readings: Read as an acted parable

The foot washing is a sign, like the signs of chapters 2–11, but acted out for the disciples alone. Laying aside his clothes and taking them up again uses the verbs of the good shepherd who lays down his life and takes it up (10:17–18). The washing pictures the cleansing his death will bring, which Peter must accept as a gift before he can pass it on.
Read as a lesson in service

Read as Jesus explains it in 13:12–17, the scene is a model. In a world that ranked everyone, the master takes the lowest place. Christians who wash feet in worship today, and those who see it as a call to humble service, both start here.
Read as a farewell

From 13:31 the chapter becomes the opening of a farewell speech, a form known from Genesis 49 and Deuteronomy. The departing leader comforts his family, gives them a command, and warns of trouble. The "new command" is the testament Jesus leaves.

views.H: John's chronology puts this meal before Passover (13:1; 18:28), not on Passover night as in Mark 14:12. Many historians think John's date is right; others think John adjusted it for theology. The scene fits first-century customs: reclining at table, foot washing by slaves, dipping bread in a shared dish, and gifts to the poor at the festival.
views.C: John has no account of the bread and cup (Mark 14:22–25), though he has bread-of-life teaching in 6:51–58. Critics ask whether the foot washing replaces the institution of the Lord's Supper in John's community, or presupposes it. The two explanations of the washing (13:6–11 and 13:12–17) may come from different stages of the Gospel's growth. The disciple Jesus loved enters here, and his role as witness raises the question of the Gospel's authorship.
views.L: Light and dark frame the chapter: Jesus knows his hour and his origin (13:1–3), and Judas walks out into the night (13:30). Misunderstanding drives the dialogue, as so often in John: Peter refuses, then overreaches. The pairing of Judas and Peter, the one who hands Jesus over and the one who denies him, sets up the passion story.
views.J: Jesus and all his disciples are Jews keeping a Jewish festival. Washing feet, reclining like free people, and giving to the poor are Jewish customs of the time. "The Jews" in 13:33 refers back to Jesus's opponents in Jerusalem (7:33–34; 8:21), not to the Jewish people, of whom the disciples are part.
views.T: The Latin of 13:34, mandatum novum, gave Maundy Thursday its name, and many churches wash feet in the Holy Thursday service. Augustine read the bath and the foot washing as baptism and daily forgiveness. Anabaptists, Brethren, Adventists and some Baptists and Pentecostals keep foot washing as an ordinance.

deep.b: John 13:31–17:26 is the longest speech of Jesus in any Gospel. It has the features of a farewell testament: the leader announces his departure (13:33), comforts his followers (14:1, 27), gives commands (13:34; 15:12), predicts trouble (15:18–16:4), names a successor (the Advocate, 14:16) and ends with a prayer (17), as Moses ends Deuteronomy with a song and blessing (Deuteronomy 32–33). Its structure is debated. Many scholars see two parallel speeches, 13:31–14:31 and 16:4b–33, which cover the same themes (going away, the Spirit, asking in his name, peace), with the vine and the world's hatred (15:1–16:4a) between them. The words "Get up. Let us leave this place" (14:31) seem to end a speech that then continues. See the note on 14:31.

deep.h: No bread and cup in John
deep.b: Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul all record Jesus's words over the bread and cup at the last supper (Mark 14:22–25; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26). John, who describes the supper at the greatest length, does not. Explanations include: John assumed his readers knew the institution and wanted to add what the others left out (Clement of Alexandria called John the "spiritual Gospel" written after the others); John placed the meaning of the Supper in chapter 6, "eat my flesh and drink my blood"; or John wanted to stress the meaning of the Lord's death, love and service, rather than the rite. Some scholars think the foot washing was itself a rite in John's community. See the topic pages on the Lord's Supper and on foot washing.

echoes: Matthew 26:20–25; Mark 14:17–21; Luke 22:14–23; Luke 22:24–27; Luke 22:31–34; Matthew 26:33–35; Psalm 41:9; Leviticus 19:18; 1 John 2:7–11; 1 John 3:16; Philippians 2:5–8; 1 Timothy 5:10

settings.what: The foot washing and its meaning
settings.to: The Twelve, including Judas, reclining at supper in Jerusalem
settings.when: the evening before Passover, the night of his arrest
settings.why: Jesus acts out, and then explains, what his coming death means for them: he cleanses them, and they must accept being served before they can serve. Then he makes the act a model: if their Lord and Teacher has done the work of a slave, they owe each other the same. Knowing that Judas is present and is washed too sharpens it: Jesus serves even the one who will hand him over.
settings.readers: For John's first readers, probably churches in the Roman province of Asia late in the first century, the scene answered the question of how to live after Jesus's departure: as a community of mutual service, cleansed by his death, under pressure from outside. Some of them may have practiced foot washing as a rite.
views: The washing points chiefly to the cross and its cleansing (Brown; Lincoln); the moral lesson follows from it.
The washing is chiefly an example, as Jesus says in 13:15; the deeper meanings are secondary (many Protestant readers).
John Christopher Thomas argues that the community practiced foot washing as a rite of forgiveness for sins after baptism.

settings.what: Jesus names the one who will hand him over
settings.to: The disciples at table; the sign is given to the disciple Jesus loved, who asked at Peter's prompting
settings.when: during the same supper, after the foot washing
settings.why: Jesus shows that he knows and is in control: Scripture has foretold it (13:18), and he tells them ahead of time so that afterward they will believe (13:19). The dipped bread, a sign of friendship, is a last gesture toward Judas; when he leaves, the hour begins.
settings.readers: Later readers struggled with how a chosen apostle could betray Jesus. John answers that Jesus was not taken by surprise and that the betrayal fulfilled Scripture, while Judas remained responsible.

settings.to: The eleven disciples, now without Judas; Peter, Thomas, Philip and the other Judas speak up
settings.when: at the supper table, after Judas has gone out into the night
settings.why: To prepare frightened disciples for his departure: he is going to the Father to prepare a place for them, he is the way, they will see the Father in him, he will send another Advocate, and he himself will come to them. He gives them the new command of love and his peace. The speech is meant to steady them before the shock of the arrest.
settings.readers: For readers who never saw Jesus, these promises explained how he remains present: through the Spirit, through love among believers, and through prayer in his name. The delay of his return is addressed by the promise of his coming to them now.
views: Traditional readers take 13:31–17:26 as a single address given at the supper or on the way to the garden.
Many critical scholars see 13:31–14:31 as the original farewell speech, with chapters 15–17 added in later editions of the Gospel (Brown; Segovia).

traditions.q: Jesus says, "you too owe it to one another to wash each other's feet" (13:14). Should churches wash feet as a rite?
views: Not as a sacrament, but as a sign. The Roman Missal includes the washing of feet in the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper, where the priest washes the feet of chosen members of the congregation; since 2016 women may be included. The rite expresses Christ's love and the call to serve.

It is not commanded as a lasting ceremony. Jesus gave an example of love and humility, which Christians follow in service. Some Lutheran churches include an optional foot washing on Maundy Thursday, as in the Evangelical Lutheran Worship service for that day.

No. Calvin wrote that Christ did not institute a yearly ceremony, and criticized the annual foot washing of his day as a theatrical show that missed the point; what Christ commands is to serve one another in love.

Yes, as an ordinance. The Dordrecht Confession (1632) teaches washing the saints' feet as Christ commanded, and Mennonite, Amish and Brethren churches practice it, often together with the Lord's Supper. The 1995 Mennonite confession calls it a sign of humble service and of the cleansing Christ gives.
Yes. Seventh-day Adventists practice the "ordinance of humility," foot washing, before every communion service, as preparation and renewal of fellowship.
Divided. Most Baptist churches keep only baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances and read 13:14 as an example. Free Will Baptists and Primitive Baptists keep foot washing as an ordinance.
Divided. The Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) lists washing the saints' feet among its ordinances; most other Pentecostal bodies, such as the Assemblies of God, do not.

title: The way to the Father's house
sum: Jesus speaks to frightened friends. He is leaving, but they must not be shaken: in his Father's house there are many places to stay, and he is going to get one ready and will come back for them. When Thomas asks the way, Jesus answers, "I am the way, the truth and the life." When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

Then come the promises. Those who believe will do greater works. Whatever they ask in his name, he will do. He will ask the Father, and the Father will give them another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will remain with them and be in them, teach them and remind them of everything. Jesus himself will come to them; he and the Father will make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word. He leaves them his peace. Then he says, "Get up. Let us leave this place."
readings: Read as comfort

Chapter 14 has been read at countless funerals for its first verses. The chapter is framed by the same words, "Your heart must not be shaken" (14:1, 27): the whole speech is meant to steady people who are about to lose their teacher.
Read as theology

Few chapters shaped Christian doctrine more. The Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, the Son who reveals the Father, and the Spirit sent by the Father in the Son's name became central texts for the doctrine of the Trinity.
Read as present hope

John shifts the expectation of Jesus's future coming toward the present: Jesus comes to his disciples after Easter, in the Spirit, and in the dwelling of the Father and Son with the believer. Many interpreters see John holding the future and the present together.

views.H: The setting is still the supper table (14:31). Thomas, Philip and Judas (not Iscariot) speak, which fits John's habit of giving minor disciples a voice (1:43–46; 11:16; 12:21–22). The promise of the Spirit reflects the experience of the early church described in Acts.
views.C: The ending of 14:31 suggests that chapter 14 once led straight to 18:1. Many critics see in the chapter John's reinterpretation of the Second Coming as Jesus's coming in the Spirit, sometimes called "realized eschatology" (Dodd; Bultmann), though the future hope remains (14:3; 5:28–29).
views.L: Each disciple's question shows a misunderstanding that Jesus uses to reveal more: Thomas wants a route, Philip a vision, Judas a public display. The word "remain" (menō) and its noun "place to stay" (monē) frame the chapter (14:2, 10, 17, 23, 25).
views.J: Jewish readers hear in "the way" the language of Torah and halakhah ("the way to walk"), and in 14:6 a sharp claim that has often been used to deny that Jews know God. Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz note the verse's exclusive tone within its setting of a community defining itself; Christian interpreters differ on what it means for Israel's covenant.
views.T: The Nicene tradition read 14:9–11 and 14:28 together: the Son is one with the Father in being and reveals him, yet the Father is the source. 14:16 and 14:26 are the ground of the church's teaching on the Spirit as a Person. In the Latin West, "many mansions" also shaped ideas of degrees of heavenly reward.

deep.b: Five sayings about the Advocate (paraklētos) are spread through the farewell speech: 14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26–27; 16:7–11; 16:12–15. Together they describe a second Advocate who takes Jesus's place: he is given by the Father at Jesus's request (14:16), sent by the Father in Jesus's name (14:26) or by Jesus from the Father (15:26; 16:7); he remains with and in the disciples (14:17); he teaches and reminds (14:26); he bears witness to Jesus alongside them (15:26–27); he puts the world on trial (16:8–11); and he guides into the truth and glorifies Jesus (16:13–14). Almost everything said of the Advocate is also said of Jesus in John, which is why Raymond Brown called the Spirit "the presence of Jesus when Jesus is absent." The title also appears in 1 John 2:1, where it is used of Jesus himself.

echoes: Exodus 33:18–23; Isaiah 43:10; Psalm 86:11; Acts 4:12; Acts 1:8; Acts 2:33; 1 John 2:1; 1 John 3:24; 1 John 4:13; Revelation 21:3; Mark 14:42; Colossians 1:15

traditions.q: "Nobody comes to the Father unless he comes through me" (14:6). Can people who have never heard of Jesus be saved?
views: Salvation always comes through Christ, but not only to those who explicitly know him. The Second Vatican Council taught that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the gospel but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will can attain eternal salvation, moved by grace (Lumen Gentium 16; Catechism 847).

Christ is the only way, and the Church is his body. Yet many Orthodox teachers refuse to say who is outside: as Kallistos Ware put it, we know where the Church is, but we cannot be sure where it is not, and God's mercy is not limited to those who know him by name.

No one is saved apart from Christ, and the Westminster Confession says those who do not profess the Christian faith cannot be saved however carefully they live by the light of nature; only elect infants and others incapable of hearing the call are saved by Christ's Spirit without the outward word.
Salvation requires personal faith in Jesus Christ as Lord. The Baptist Faith and Message says there is no salvation apart from personal faith in Jesus, which is why missions are urgent.

Divided. Wesley taught that God's grace is at work in every person before they hear the gospel, and he hoped that those who never heard would be judged by the light they had; many Methodists today hold a hopeful view, while others insist on explicit faith.

traditions.q: "The Father is greater than I am" (14:28). Is the Son less than the Father?
views: The Son is equal to the Father in being, as the Nicene Creed confesses. The fathers gave two answers that Orthodox and Catholics share: the Father is "greater" as the source from whom the Son is eternally begotten, not in nature (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 30, who also allows the next answer), or Jesus speaks as man (Cyril of Alexandria).

The same Nicene faith as the Orthodox, with the same two explanations (Hilary used the first). Augustine stressed the second: as man the Son is less than the Father, and he speaks here in his human nature, which he took when he "emptied himself" (Augustine, On the Trinity 1.7; the Athanasian Creed: "equal to the Father as touching his Godhead, and inferior to the Father as touching his manhood").

The same Nicene faith: the Son is of one substance with the Father, and the verse speaks of his role as the Mediator who was sent. Calvin read it of Christ in his office as Mediator, not of his divine being.
The Son is a created being, God's first creation, and this verse is plain evidence that Jehovah is greater than Jesus. The doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Bible.
The Father and the Son are separate, distinct beings, one in purpose. The Father is greater, and the Son is fully subject to him.

title: The vine and the world
sum: "I am the real vine, and my Father is the farmer." Jesus takes the old picture of Israel as God's vine and applies it to himself. The disciples are branches. The Father removes the fruitless ones and trims the fruitful ones clean. The one command is to remain: remain in me, remain in my love. Without him they can do nothing; joined to him they bear much fruit, and their prayers are answered.

Remaining in his love means keeping his command to love one another as he loved them, to the point of laying down life for friends. They are no longer slaves but friends, and they did not choose him; he chose them. Then the tone changes. The world that hated Jesus will hate them, because they do not belong to it. But the Advocate will come, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, and he will bear witness about Jesus, and so will they.
readings: Read as Israel's story

In the Old Testament, Israel is the vine God planted (Psalm 80; Isaiah 5). Jesus is the true vine: Israel's calling and life are summed up in him, and his disciples, all of them Jews at this point, are the branches of the renewed people.
Read as spiritual life
Christian devotion has treasured this chapter as a picture of union with Christ. "Remain" invites settled trust rather than anxious effort; the fruit comes from staying joined to the vine.
Read as community
The branches are plural, and the fruit is love for each other. The vine is a community image as much as a personal one: the church is the vine's branches together, facing a hostile world together.

views.H: Vineyards covered the hills of Judea, and the golden vine on the Temple gate was famous. By John's time, Christians in Asia Minor knew hostility from neighbors and synagogues and sometimes Roman trials. The warnings of 15:18–16:4 matched their experience.
views.C: Many critics see chapters 15–16 as a second layer of the farewell speech, added after 14:31. The vine passage has no Synoptic parallel except the parable of the vineyard tenants (Mark 12:1–12). The Spirit sayings in 15:26–27 interrupt the theme of hatred and may be placed here to show the Spirit as the disciples' defense.
views.L: The repeated word "remain" (ten times in 15:1–10, eleven in 15:1–17) gives the passage a slow, circling rhythm. "Love" and "hate" divide the chapter into two halves: the love inside the vine and the hatred of the world outside.
views.J: The vine was a national symbol of Israel on coins of the Jewish revolts and on the Temple. Claiming to be "the real vine" sets Jesus in Israel's place. "Their law" (15:25) and the world's hatred have been read against the Jewish people; Jewish and Christian scholars today stress that John speaks of a conflict inside the Jewish world of his day.
views.T: 15:26 is the verse behind the creed's "who proceeds from the Father," and the center of the Filioque dispute between East and West. 15:6 is a key text in the debate over whether believers can fall away. The image of the vine was loved in early Christian art and liturgy.

deep.b: The Creed of Nicaea, as expanded at Constantinople in 381, says the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father," using the verb of 15:26. In the Latin West, partly to guard the Son's full divinity against Arian views, churches began to say the Spirit proceeds "from the Father and the Son" (filioque). The phrase was added to the creed in Spain at the Third Council of Toledo (589), spread in the Frankish empire, and was adopted at Rome in the early 1000s. Patriarch Photius of Constantinople (about 867) attacked it as both a change to an ecumenical creed and a theological error. It became one of the causes of the split between Eastern and Western churches in 1054. The Council of Florence (1439) tried to reconcile the two by explaining that the Spirit proceeds from the Father "through the Son," but the union did not last. In modern dialogue some Western churches have printed the creed without the phrase, and the Vatican (1995) affirmed that the Father alone is the source of the Spirit in the Greek sense of ekporeusis.

echoes: Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15:1–8; Ezekiel 19:10–14; Hosea 10:1; Mark 12:1–12; Matthew 10:17–25; Psalm 35:19; Psalm 69:4; 1 John 3:13–16; 1 John 4:7–12; Romans 11:17–24; Exodus 33:11; Isaiah 41:8

settings.when: on the last night, either still at the supper or on the way out of the city (14:31; 18:1)
settings.why: To show the disciples that their life and fruitfulness after his departure depend entirely on staying joined to him, and that this union shows itself in obeying his command to love one another. The warning about fruitless branches, spoken just after Judas has left, makes clear that outward closeness is not enough.
settings.readers: For John's churches, the vine described what it meant to belong to the true people of God when they were no longer welcome in the synagogue: they were Israel's branches by being in Jesus.
views: Most read the vine as an extended metaphor, like the good shepherd (10:1–18), not a parable with a story.
Some read it as an echo of the cup of the Lord's Supper, "the produce of the vine" (Mark 14:25), as many fathers did.

settings.when: the same night, hours before his arrest
settings.why: To warn them ahead of time that they will be hated, expelled and even killed by people who think they serve God, so that when it happens they will not be tripped up but will remember that he told them. It also assures them that they will not testify alone: the Advocate will testify with them.
settings.readers: The Gospel's first readers knew expulsion from synagogues and pressure from Roman authorities. These words gave meaning to their suffering: they shared the fate of their master.
views: Martyn and others read 16:2 as reflecting a formal break between synagogues and Jesus-believers late in the first century.
Others think the hostility was local and occasional, and that John generalizes it (Kimelman; Reinhartz).

traditions.q: "Whoever does not remain in me is tossed out like the branch" (15:6). Can a true believer fall away and be lost?
views: Yes. Grace received can be lost through mortal sin, and so can salvation, unless a person repents. Trent taught that no one can be certain without a special revelation that they will persevere to the end.
Yes. Salvation is a life of union with Christ that must be lived out to the end; a person can turn away from it. The warning of the cut-off branch is real.
Yes. The Augsburg Confession rejects the view that those once justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit. Believers can fall from grace through unbelief, but can be restored by repentance.

No. Those God has truly joined to Christ will persevere to the end, kept by God's power (Westminster Confession 17). The burned branch is someone outwardly attached to Christ, like Judas, who never had real life from the vine.
Yes. Wesley argued from this very passage that a real branch of the true vine can be cut off and cast into the fire, so believers must remain in Christ.
No, for most Baptists. The Baptist Faith and Message teaches that genuine believers will never fall away finally; Free Will Baptists, however, teach that a believer can turn away and be lost.

traditions.q: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father" (15:26). Does the Spirit proceed from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son?
views: From the Father alone, the one source in the Godhead. The Spirit is sent in time by the Son (15:26; 16:7), but his eternal origin is the Father, as the creed of 381 says. Adding "and the Son" to the creed without an ecumenical council was wrong, and the doctrine confuses the Persons (Photius).

From the Father and the Son as from one principle. The Father is the first origin; the Son shares in the procession because everything the Father has belongs to the Son (16:15). The Eastern phrase "from the Father through the Son" expresses the same faith when rightly understood (Council of Florence; Catechism 246–248).
From the Father and the Son. The Lutheran confessions accept the Western creeds, including the Athanasian Creed, which says the Spirit is "of the Father and of the Son."
From the Father and the Son. The Westminster Confession says the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Thirty-Nine Articles say the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. But the Lambeth Conference of 1978 asked Anglican churches to consider printing the Nicene Creed without the Filioque, out of respect for the Orthodox, and some now do.

title: Grief that turns to joy
sum: Jesus finishes his warning: they will be thrown out of the synagogue, and some who kill them will think they are serving God. He tells them now so that they will not be tripped up. Grief fills their hearts, but he insists that his going is for their good, because only then will the Advocate come. The Spirit will put the world on trial over sin, righteousness and judgment, and will guide the disciples in all the truth, taking what belongs to Jesus and making it known.

"A short time, and you no longer see me. Then a short time again, and you will see me." The disciples are puzzled. Jesus compares their coming grief to a woman in labor whose pain turns to joy when the child is born. On that day they will ask the Father in his name, for the Father himself loves them. The disciples declare they finally understand and believe. Jesus warns that within hours they will scatter and leave him alone, yet he is not alone. His last words to them: "In the world you have hardship. But be brave: I have won the victory over the world."
readings: Read as the Spirit's work

Chapter 16 holds the fullest teaching about the Advocate in the Gospels: he convicts the world and guides the church. Much Christian thinking about how the Spirit works, in conscience, in preaching and in the church's understanding of Scripture, starts here.
Read as Easter
The "short time" sayings point first to Good Friday and Easter: grief for three days, then joy no one can take away. The birth image says the cross is not the end but the labor that brings new life.
Read as the church's life between the times
Many readers hear the whole age of the church in this chapter: a time of hardship, of prayer in Jesus's name, of the Spirit's witness, lived in peace because the decisive victory is already won.

views.H: The warnings about expulsion and violence fit the experience of the first Christians, from Stephen to the persecutions under Nero and, many think, Domitian, and the local tensions in Asia Minor that Revelation 2:9 and 3:9 also reflect.
views.C: 16:4b–33 repeats themes of chapter 14 (the departure, the Spirit, asking in his name, peace) and seems unaware that Thomas and Peter already asked where Jesus was going (16:5). Many scholars think it is a parallel version of the farewell speech.
views.L: The chapter turns on contrasts: grief and joy, a short time and a short time, word pictures and plain speech, scattering and not being alone, hardship in the world and peace in him. The disciples' overconfident "Now we can tell" (16:30) is a final misunderstanding before the arrest.
views.J: 16:2 is one of the three passages about expulsion from the synagogue that shaped the theory of a sharp Jewish-Christian break in the late first century. Jewish scholars point out how these verses, read without history, have cast Jews as persecutors, though for most of later history Christians held power over Jews.
views.T: 16:7–15 is central for Christian teaching on the Spirit, and 16:13 for debates over how the church's teaching develops and who interprets Scripture. Augustine and the Latin tradition drew on 16:14–15 for the Filioque.

echoes: Isaiah 26:17–19; Isaiah 66:7–14; Zechariah 13:7; Mark 13:8–13; Mark 14:27; Matthew 10:17–22; Acts 26:9–11; 1 John 5:4–5; Revelation 12:2; Romans 8:22–27; 1 Corinthians 2:10–13

settings.what: The second farewell speech (from 16:4b): the Spirit and the short time
settings.when: the last night, before he leaves with them for the garden across the Kidron (18:1)
settings.why: To turn the disciples' grief toward hope: his going is for their good, the Spirit will come to continue his work and guide them, their sorrow will soon turn into lasting joy, and they will have direct access to the Father in prayer. It ends with a frank warning that they will fail him that very night, and a word of peace so that their failure will not destroy them.
settings.readers: Readers in John's churches lived after Easter, in the time of the Spirit, of prayer in Jesus's name, and of hardship in the world. The speech told them that this was the life Jesus had foreseen and promised, not a sign that he had abandoned them.
views: Traditional readers see one speech that develops its themes.
Many critical scholars see a second form of the farewell speech, treasured and placed beside the first (Brown).

traditions.q: "He will lead you in all the truth" (16:13). Does the Spirit guide the church's teaching beyond Scripture?
views: Yes. The promise was given to the apostles and continues in the church: the Spirit guides the bishops in communion with the pope, so that the church's teaching office faithfully interprets the word of God handed down in Scripture and Tradition (Catechism 85–95; Vatican II, Dei Verbum).
Yes. The Spirit guides the whole church, bishops and people together, and his guidance is seen above all in the ecumenical councils and the living Tradition, of which Scripture is the heart.
The promise was fulfilled in the apostles, whose teaching is preserved in Scripture. Scripture alone is the rule by which all teachers and teachings are judged; councils can err.

The Spirit led the apostles into all truth, and their witness is written in Scripture. The same Spirit illuminates believers to understand it, but adds no new revelation, and all church decisions are to be tested by Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10).

The church has authority in controversies of faith, but it may not teach anything contrary to Scripture, and general councils can err and have erred; what they decide binds only if it can be shown from Scripture (Articles 20–21).
The Spirit still speaks and guides believers today through gifts such as prophecy, but every word is tested by Scripture, the infallible rule of faith and conduct.

title: The prayer of the hour
sum: Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. The hour has come. He asks the Father to glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify him, and to restore the glory he had beside the Father before there was a world. Eternal life, he says, is to know the only real God and the one he sent.

Then he prays for the disciples the Father gave him. He has kept them and guarded them; only the son of ruin was lost. Now he is going, and they remain in a world that hates them. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but that they be kept from the evil one and made holy in the truth, because he is sending them as he was sent. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their word: that they may all be one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world will believe. He wants them to be with him and to see his glory, and he promises to keep making the Father's name known, so that the Father's love will be in them, and he in them.
readings: Read as the High Priest's prayer

Jesus consecrates himself as an offering (17:19) and intercedes for his people, like the high priest on the Day of Atonement who prayed for himself, his household and all Israel (Leviticus 16:17). Hebrews develops the same picture (Hebrews 7:25).
Read as the prayer for unity
Much of the modern ecumenical movement took its mandate from 17:21. The unity Jesus prays for is modeled on the life of the Trinity and aimed at the world's faith.
Read as the Gospel in miniature

Nearly every theme of John returns here: the hour, glory, the Son sent by the Father, eternal life as knowledge, the name, the world, truth, love, and unity. The prayer gathers the whole Gospel and turns it toward the cross.

views.H: Whether a disciple could have remembered a long prayer word for word is doubtful. Defenders of its historical root note that Jesus prayed aloud before his arrest in the other Gospels (Mark 14:32–36) and that the prayer echoes the Lord's Prayer: Father, the name, the will, protection from the evil one.
views.C: Most critical scholars see the prayer as the evangelist's composition in Jesus's voice, a summary of the Gospel's theology. The speaker seems already beyond the cross ("I am no longer in the world," 17:11; "I glorified you," 17:4), as if the risen Christ were praying.
views.L: The prayer moves in widening circles: the Son and the Father, the disciples, all future believers, and the world. Repeated words (give, glory, world, name, one, love) weave it together. It is the climax of the farewell speech and the threshold of the passion.
views.J: The prayer has many Jewish features: addressing God as Father, sanctifying the name, the world to come as knowing God. Its claim that the Son shared the Father's glory before creation is where Jewish and Christian readers part ways most clearly.
views.T: The prayer is read in many churches during the Easter season and at ordinations. It has been central for the doctrine of the Trinity, for theosis in the Orthodox Church, and for twentieth-century ecumenism.

deep.h: The prayer and the Lord's Prayer
deep.b: John has no Lord's Prayer, but John 17 shares many of its themes. Both address God as "Father" (Matthew 6:9; 17:1). Both are concerned with God's name: "May your name be kept holy" and "I have brought your name into the open" (17:6, 26). Both ask for God's will and glory on earth (17:4). Both ask for protection from "the evil one" (Matthew 6:13; 17:15). Some scholars think John 17 is a meditation on the Lord's Prayer, or that both draw on the same Jewish prayer patterns, such as the Kaddish, which begins by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified in the world he created.

echoes: Leviticus 16:17; Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 6:4; Jeremiah 31:34; Proverbs 8:22–31; Isaiah 42:8; Isaiah 52:6; Matthew 6:9–13; Hebrews 7:25; Hebrews 10:10; Ephesians 1:4; Ephesians 4:3–6; 1 John 1:3; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; Didache 10:2

settings.to: The Father, spoken aloud in the hearing of the eleven disciples
settings.when: at the end of the farewell speech, just before they cross the Kidron to the garden where he is arrested (18:1)
settings.why: To commit himself, his disciples and all future believers into the Father's hands at the moment of the hour. Spoken aloud, it also teaches the disciples what he is doing and what they are for: they are kept, made holy and sent, so that the world may believe. Knowing that they heard it changes its force: the frightened men who will scatter that night (16:32) hear Jesus asking the Father to keep them.
settings.readers: For John's readers, "those who believe in me through what they say" (17:20) meant themselves. The prayer assured them that Jesus had prayed for them by name, as it were, and that their unity and love were part of his mission to the world.
views: Traditional readers take it as the substance of Jesus's prayer that night, remembered by the Beloved Disciple.
Most critical scholars see it as John's own composition, a prayer of the exalted Christ summing up the Gospel (Käsemann called it Jesus's "testament").
